\section[\texorpdfstring{\fa{کمردرد} (kamardard)}{کمردرد (kamardard)}]{\fa{کمردرد} (kamardard) — backache, lower back pain}

\label{lesson:FA-C491-kamardard}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Persian for a sore throat, then the Persian for to run a fever.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \fa{کمردرد}}
\textbf{\fa{کمردرد}} (\emph{kamardard}) — \textquotedblleft{}backache, lower back pain\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
\fa{پدرم} \fa{بعد} \fa{از} \fa{کار} \fa{در} \fa{باغ} \fa{کمردرد} \fa{گرفت}.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{pedaram ba'd az kâr dar bâgh kamardard gereft.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
My father got backache after working in the garden.
\end{quote}

\emph{kamar} 'lower back, waist' + \emph{dard} 'pain'. \emph{kamardard gereftan} — to get backache.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{kamardard} is built on two inherited words: \emph{kamar}, 'waist, lower back', which EtymDB traces to Middle Persian (EtymDB), and \emph{dard}, 'pain'.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{kamardard}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{kamardard}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{kamardard}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Persian for a sore throat, then the Persian for to run a fever, then say \emph{kamardard} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \fa{کمردرد} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}Backache, lower back pain\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.

\section[\texorpdfstring{\fa{دندان} \fa{درد} (dandân dard)}{دندان درد (dandân dard)}]{\fa{دندان} \fa{درد} (dandân dard) — toothache}

\label{lesson:FA-C491-dandan-dard}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Persian for to run a fever, then the Persian for backache.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \fa{دندان} \fa{درد}}
\textbf{\fa{دندان} \fa{درد}} (\emph{dandân dard}) — \textquotedblleft{}toothache\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
\fa{با} \fa{دندان} \fa{درد} \fa{به} \fa{دندانپزشک} \fa{رفتم}.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{bâ dandân dard be dandânpezeshk raftam.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
I went to the dentist with toothache.
\end{quote}

\emph{dandân} 'tooth' + \emph{dard} 'pain'. In speech also \emph{dandun dard}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{dandân dard} is built on two inherited words. \emph{dandân}, 'tooth', comes from Middle Persian, and EtymDB lists Latin \emph{dens} and Greek \emph{odous} as its cousins (EtymDB); \emph{dard} is 'pain'.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\fa{درد} \fa{کشیدن} (dard keshidan)}{درد کشیدن (dard keshidan)}]{\fa{درد} \fa{کشیدن} (dard keshidan) — to suffer pain}

\label{lesson:FA-C491-dard-keshidan}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Persian for backache, then the Persian for toothache.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \fa{درد} \fa{کشیدن}}
\textbf{\fa{درد} \fa{کشیدن}} (\emph{dard keshidan}) — \textquotedblleft{}to suffer pain\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
\fa{او} \fa{سالها} \fa{درد} \fa{کشید}.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{u sâlhâ dard keshid.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
She suffered pain for years.
\end{quote}

\emph{dard} 'pain' + \emph{keshidan} 'to pull, to bear'; present stem \emph{kesh-}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{dard keshidan} is built on two inherited Persian words, \emph{dard}, 'pain', and \emph{keshidan}, 'to pull, to bear': to bear pain.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.

\section[\texorpdfstring{\fa{خارش} (khâresh)}{خارش (khâresh)}]{\fa{خارش} (khâresh) — an itch, itching}

\label{lesson:FA-C491-kharesh}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Persian for toothache, then the Persian for to suffer pain.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \fa{خارش}}
\textbf{\fa{خارش}} (\emph{khâresh}) — \textquotedblleft{}an itch, itching\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
\fa{دستم} \fa{خارش} \fa{دارد}.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{dastam khâresh dârad.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
My hand itches.
\end{quote}

The noun from \emph{khâridan} 'to itch' (stem \emph{khâr-}) with \emph{-esh}; \emph{khârândan} is 'to scratch'. \emph{khâresh dâshtan} — to itch.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{khâresh} is built on \emph{khâr-}, the present stem of the native verb \emph{khâridan}, 'to itch', with the noun ending \emph{-esh}. EtymDB has no entry for it.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\fa{سکسکه} \fa{کردن} (sekseke kardan)}{سکسکه کردن (sekseke kardan)}]{\fa{سکسکه} \fa{کردن} (sekseke kardan) — to hiccup}

\label{lesson:FA-C491-sekseke-kardan}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Persian for to suffer pain, then the Persian for an itch.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \fa{سکسکه} \fa{کردن}}
\textbf{\fa{سکسکه} \fa{کردن}} (\emph{sekseke kardan}) — \textquotedblleft{}to hiccup\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
\fa{بچه} \fa{بعد} \fa{از} \fa{غذا} \fa{سکسکه} \fa{میکند}.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{bachche ba'd az ghazâ sekseke mikonad.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
The baby hiccups after eating.
\end{quote}

\emph{sekseke} 'hiccup' + \emph{kardan}; present stem \emph{kon-}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{sekseke} is usually explained as imitative, built on the sound of a hiccup itself, and \emph{kardan}, 'to do', is inherited Persian. EtymDB has no entry for it.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}
